To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
exposure of dairy heifers to 50 lux at night for 8 hr significantly suppressed melatonin levels for 2 hr but not thereafter.
dim light exposure at night (5 lx, 10 lx and 50 lx) had no effect on plasma melatonin or insulin‐like growth factors in prepubertal dairy heifers.
exposure to 5 and10 lx had little effect on NML in prepubertal dairy heifers, but that exposure to 50 1× suppressed NML for the first 2 hr after the onset of night treatment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of artificial light at night in barns and the effect of this light on the melatonin cycle of dairy cattle.
the effects of light at night on melatonin and IGF‐ 1.
the effects of light at night on melatonin and growth in dairy heifers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

exposure of prepubertal heifers to 50 lxsuppressed NML during the initial 1–2 hr of night and this effect was consistent throughout the 14 days of the study, but that exposure of heifers to 5 or 10 lx did not alter NML.
exposure to 50 1lx of light at night suppressed NML for the first 2 hr, and had no effect thereafter, and that plasma IGF‐I level was higher in period 4 than in period 3.

exposure of prepubertal dairy heifers to 50 1× light during the night for 8 hr suppressed melatonin secretion for the first 2 hr but did not suppress it for the rest of the night, and did not affect plasma IGF‐ 1 level.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
exposure to 10 lx at night does not affect NML or plasma IGF‐ 1 level in prepubertal heifers.

the use of 10 1x of light at night does not affect the melatonin rhythm and that the use of a higher level of light at night (50 1x in our case) may suppress melatonin for a short time but does not affect the overall melatonin pattern during the night.
the use of dim light in barns during the night may be beneficial to dairy heifers by increasing plasma IGF‐I levels and may be detrimental to dairy heifers because of suppression of NML.
The main takeaway from our work is that
dim light does not affect the nocturnal rise of IGF‐1, and that the nocturnal rise in IGF‐1 is not dependent on the nocturnal rise melatonin.
the light intensities that we tested (5, 50 lx) had little effect on NML, and that the light intensity used in this experiment (50 lx) did not have an effect on plasma IGH‐1 levels.
dim light at night (10 and 5 lx) does not suppress NML and may therefore be safe to use in barns where darkness during the night is recommended.
